title: Know the Design, and You Will Know the Designer
note: Scripture quotations are from the Berean Standard Bible (public domain) unless otherwise noted.
sources: Barthlott, Wilhelm; Neinhuis, Christoph, Purity of the Sacred Lotus, or Escape from Contamination in Biological Surfaces, “Planta” 202 (1997)
Bryson, Bill, The Body: A Guide for Occupants, Doubleday 2019
Keltner, Dacher, Awe: The New Science of Everyday Wonder and How It Can Transform Your Life, Penguin Press 2023
Keltner, Dacher; Haidt, Jonathan, Approaching Awe, a Moral, Spiritual, and Aesthetic Emotion, “Cognition and Emotion” 17 (2003)
Piff, Paul K.; Dietze, Pia; Feinberg, Matthew; Stancato, Daniel M.; Keltner, Dacher, Awe, the Small Self, and Prosocial Behavior, “Journal of Personality and Social Psychology” 108 (2015)
Sturm, Virginia E. et al., Big Smile, Small Self: Awe Walks Promote Prosocial Positive Emotions in Older Adults, “Emotion”, published online 2020

paragraphs: One day a Swiss engineer came home from a hunt covered in burdock burrs. But instead of throwing them away, as he did after every outing, he put one of them under a microscope. To his surprise, he saw a thicket of springy little hooks that easily caught on every loop in the fabric. After years of trial and error, he patented a system based on a similar mechanism, and so the fastener we now know as Velcro was born. Whole generations before him had pulled the same burrs out of their sleeves and their dogs’ fur, but no one had looked at them long enough to understand how the mechanism worked and put it to everyday use.

The brain has a good reason not to analyze everything. It pushes whatever is familiar into the background so that it can save its attention for new experiences. As a result, over the years we stop noticing the things we brush against every day. Small children ask questions endlessly; adults rarely do. We lose our capacity for wonder without noticing as life goes on, but that too can change if we work at it consciously.

Experiencing awe shifts our inner perspective, drawing our attention away from our own problems and making us more sensitive to other people. Research by psychologist Dacher Keltner at the University of California, Berkeley showed that people who spent a minute gazing at the crowns of tall trees were afterwards more willing to help others than those who had stared at the wall of a building. But Keltner went further and analyzed how people experience awe, drawing on stories sent in from 26 different countries. The result? Nothing moves us as deeply as the sight of someone else’s kindness or courage.

Three thousand years ago, near Bethlehem, the shepherd David spent his nights with his flock under a sky strewn with thousands of stars. In Psalm 8 he calls that starry sky “the work of Your fingers” and asks in wonder: “what is man that You are mindful of him?” Yet this question about human frailty leads to a surprising paradox: this speck lost in the cosmos turns out to be someone the Creator never stops remembering.

One day Jesus was speaking to people worn out by the daily worry of putting food on the table and clothes on their backs, and He pointed them to the birds of the air and the lilies of the field. He wanted them to see the Father’s care in creation and to learn to rely on Him. For Jesus, looking closely at creation was the beginning of a path to deep trust, not just a way to find a moment’s calm.
The world is full of effortless beauty. For David, it is a trace of the Creator’s generosity, an invitation to get to know His character more and more closely.
Prepared by: Marek Micyk
Content editor: Beata Dutkowska

questions: What did I miss today because I thought it was too ordinary?
challenge: Here is a task for you. Before you put down your phone or switch off your computer, stop for a moment. Think of one thing you only glanced at today, and this time give it more of your attention. Try to notice what isn’t obvious, and then share what you noticed with someone.

paragraphs: In the autumn of 1941, Swiss engineer Georges de Mestral came back from a hunting trip in the Alps with his dog. As after every such outing, he set about picking burdock burrs off his trousers and out of the dog’s fur. He had probably done it a hundred times before, but this time, instead of simply throwing them away, he decided to look under magnification at why they clung to the fabric so firmly. He took one of the burrs to his workshop, put it under a microscope, and saw a thicket of tiny, springy hooks, each one catching on a loop of fiber. A dozen or so years later, de Mestral patented a fastener made of two strips: one covered with hooks, the other with loops. This is the invention we know today as Velcro, used just about everywhere. The company de Mestral founded after patenting it outlived its founder and still exists today.

This story is usually told as an anecdote about the birth of a brilliant idea, but its real point lies elsewhere. Before de Mestral, whole generations of people had pulled burrs out of their clothes and their dogs’ fur. The idea was within arm’s reach, yet it was noticed only by someone who took the trouble to look more closely at something trivial and obvious.
If it was all lying right there in plain sight, why did no one see it for so long? And how many similar things do we walk past every day simply because they seem too ordinary to us?

sections.heading: Everything Has Already Been Invented
paragraphs: The story of Velcro is not an isolated case. Drawing on the wisdom of nature and carrying its mechanisms over into the world of technology even has an official name: biomimetics.

In the 1990s, Japan’s high-speed shinkansen trains faced a serious problem. A train entering a tunnel at enormous speed pushed a mass of compressed air ahead of it, which burst out of the far end with a loud boom that plagued the people living nearby. One of the engineers, a keen birdwatcher, was inspired by the kingfisher, which dives into water to hunt with barely a splash, and he proposed a revolutionary solution. When, in 1997, the front of the train was lengthened into the shape of a bird’s beak, the troublesome boom disappeared, and the train’s aerodynamics improved so much that its electricity consumption fell as well.

The lotus leaf, though it grows out of mud and silt, always stays spotlessly clean. This is thanks to microscopic bumps that make drops of water roll across its surface like perfect little beads, picking up every bit of dirt on the way. German botanists studied the phenomenon under an electron microscope and described it in 1997. The name “lotus effect” quickly made its way into industry: modern facade paints and self-cleaning glass work on the same principle today.

But the most finely crafted design of all is the one you carry inside you. In his book on how the human body works, Bill Bryson lists a whole series of biological marvels we walk past every day without a second thought. In almost every cell of your body lie two copies of DNA, each about a meter long when unwound, and both fit inside a nucleus invisible to the naked eye. Your heart will beat roughly a hundred thousand times today, and it will adjust its pace by itself depending on whether you are climbing the stairs or falling asleep. Your brain, with around 86 billion neurons, will use a fifth of your body’s total energy over the course of a day, about four hundred kilocalories. And the cartilage at the base of your thumb is smoother than glass and glides over itself more easily than a skate on ice, because its friction is five times lower. Our bodies are full of microscopic wonders, even though in the rush of everyday life we take them completely for granted.

sections.heading: Why Do We Stop Seeing?
paragraphs: Most of us pass all of this by with a shrug, and there is a psychological explanation for that. Scientists call the phenomenon habituation. The brain pushes into the background whatever is constant and familiar, so that it can focus on what is new and important. Thanks to this, you don’t have to work out afresh every morning how the door handle works. The price of this autopilot, however, is that over the years we stop noticing the things we meet every day, even our own hands, which have been with us since birth.

Small children ask questions endlessly, and many of them begin with “why?” Adults, meanwhile, do so remarkably rarely. The capacity for awe and wonder is easily lost, and getting it back takes constant practice.

sections.heading: A Minute Under the Eucalyptus Trees
paragraphs: American psychologist Dacher Keltner has been studying the experience of awe for more than twenty years. According to his definition, formulated in 2003, awe arises when we encounter something that surpasses us in size or power. It might be a majestic mountain range, but it might just as well be someone’s courage. At the same time, the experience goes beyond our existing mental frameworks, which forces our mind to rebuild them.

In 2015, Keltner’s team at the University of California, Berkeley carried out a simple but remarkably telling experiment. The researchers divided students into two groups: the first spent 60 seconds looking up at the crowns of the towering eucalyptus trees growing on campus, while the second stared at the plain wall of a nearby building. A moment later, an assistant walking past the participants pretended to stumble and spilled a whole box of pens on the ground. The result was clear: those who had looked at the trees were more willing to help pick them up, and did so more often.

In other studies in the same series, people who had just experienced a moment of awe said they felt small in the face of what surrounded them, and their own concerns seemed less important than usual. Keltner called this the “small self” effect. Awe changes our perspective completely. It does not belittle or humiliate anyone. It simply means that our own “self” stops filling the whole frame, and other people come into view.

The same team collected some 2,600 accounts of awe from people in 26 countries. You might expect its most common source to be landscapes and works of art, yet what moved people most often was the kindness and courage of others. When the researchers looked more closely at these stories, it turned out that in most cases what had moved people was simply another person’s selfless act. The results of any single psychological experiment should always be treated with some caution, but in this case the direction of the findings has been consistently confirmed by research teams around the world.

sections.heading: A Shepherd Under the Stars
paragraphs: Three thousand years earlier, David described the same experience. Before he became king, as the youngest son of Jesse, he tended sheep near Bethlehem, spending his nights under the open sky in a darkness untouched by city lights. The fire burned low, the sheep slept, and thousands of stars hung over the hills of Judah. It may well have been in circumstances like these that Psalm 8 was written.

David had no telescope. Today we know that the naked eye can see barely a few thousand of the hundreds of billions of stars in our galaxy, and that there are more galaxies than we can count. Yet in those three thousand years, his question has lost none of its sharpness.

David writes that when he looks at the sky, “the work of Your fingers, the moon and the stars,” he asks himself: “what is man that You are mindful of him?” The very choice of words carries a deeper message. The sky that so overwhelms him he calls the work of God’s fingers, while just a few verses later he describes the earth and the animals entrusted to humankind as “the works of Your hands.” The psalmist does not develop this comparison explicitly, but the image of fingers highlights God’s craftsmanship. Seen this way, the vastness that dwarfs human beings turns out to be the work of an exceptionally careful Maker.

David’s first reaction is precisely that sense of a “small self”: what is a human being in the face of such a boundless universe? Yet the psalmist does not stop at the sense of his own frailty. This microscopic creature turns out to be someone the Creator never stops remembering. The next verse says that God made man “a little lower than God” (WEB) and crowned him with glory and honor. Awe lets us see our own modest size as it really is, and the psalm brings a comforting answer: in all this immensity, no one has forgotten us.

The structure of the whole psalm is fascinating, too. It begins and ends with exactly the same sentence: “O LORD, our Lord, how majestic is Your name in all the earth!” Humanity stands at the very center of this structure, surrounded on both sides by God’s name. And at the beginning of the psalm there is one more surprising statement: God establishes strength “from the lips of babes and infants” (WEB), the very ones who keep asking “why?” and still have a pure capacity for wonder.

Many centuries later, on one of the hills of Galilee, Jesus spoke to ordinary people who were paralyzed by worry about food and clothing for the next day. In Matthew’s Gospel He says, “Look at the birds of the air,” and a moment later He points to the lilies growing wild in the field. Instead of complicated calming techniques, Jesus gives His listeners something far simpler: He turns their eyes to nature, so that they can see in it the Father’s hidden care. On His lips, attentive observation of creation becomes the foundation of a call to deep trust.

sections.heading: What Follows from This?
paragraphs: Know the design, and you know the Designer. The title of this chapter is more an invitation to a certain way of seeing the world than a mathematical proof. A burr will not force anyone to believe, after all, and honest observation also sees predation, disease, and pain in nature. Awe does not answer every question, but it teaches us the attentiveness without which it is hard even to begin looking for answers. Faith rarely begins with a logical argument. More often it is born of an alert attention that lets us ask the right question: Who could have wanted the world to be just like this? We are free to leave that question open, and to keep coming back to it for the rest of our lives.

A lotus leaf could be ugly and still do its engineering job, and a kingfisher could catch fish in plain gray feathers. For David, the beauty and order of the world point to the Creator’s generosity, and although they do not remove the questions about suffering, they encourage us to get to know His character more closely.

There is also a challenge here for our generation. The screen in your pocket delivers something new every few seconds, and a brain with habituation permanently built in quickly learns to scroll through content without thinking. Novelty without depth gives a brief lift, but it does not give awe. Awe takes time spent under the trees or under the stars, and sometimes simply a second look at an unremarkable burr. Today such moments have to be planned deliberately, because they happen on their own less and less often.
Awe also changes the way we see ourselves. It lets us see our own worries in a wider perspective, and Psalm 8 reminds us how much a human being is worth and that God remembers us.

Content editor: Beata Dutkowska

questions: What did I fail to notice today because it seemed too ordinary?
challenge: **In your thoughts.** Recall one thing you looked at today without giving it much attention. Perhaps it was the mug in your hand, the light coming through the window, or the face of someone close to you. Bring that image back once more and stay with it for a moment, even just ten seconds longer than usual. Try to see what slipped past your attention before.

**In action.** Go for a fifteen-minute walk with one task: find something you cannot fully explain. It might be a bud on a branch, the pattern of the clouds, or the way an elderly person moves. You don’t need to go far: a park, a backyard, a bus stop, or the view from a bus window is enough. Take out your phone only once, to take a single photo. In the evening, show it to someone and tell them what caught your attention or what surprised you. For awe has a special quality: when we share it, it does not shrink but grows. And if you have no one to show the photo to today, send it to someone you haven’t talked to in a long time.
